profile.headline: Effectively 100% fatal once clinical, yet entirely preventable by prompt post-exposure prophylaxis; ~59,000 deaths annually, mostly from dog bites.
profile.syndrome: Prodromal pain or paraesthesia at the bite site, then either encephalitic ('furious') rabies with hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation and autonomic instability, or paralytic ('dumb') rabies mimicking Guillain–Barré syndrome. Death follows within days to weeks.
profile.transmission: Saliva of an infected mammal through a bite, scratch or mucosal contact; rare transmission by corneal and solid-organ transplantation and by aerosol in bat caves and laboratories.
profile.reservoir: Domestic dogs in most of Asia and Africa; bats, raccoons, skunks and foxes in the Americas and Europe.
profile.geography: Worldwide except a few island nations and Antarctica.
profile.incubation: Typically 1–3 months, ranging from days to over a year depending on inoculum and bite site.
profile.diagnosis: Ante-mortem: saliva RT-PCR (serial samples), nuchal skin biopsy, corneal impression. Post-mortem: direct fluorescent antibody on brain, Negri bodies.
profile.management: No proven treatment once symptomatic; the Milwaukee protocol is not supported by evidence. Care is palliative.
profile.prevention: Immediate and thorough wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin infiltration plus vaccine series for category III exposures, pre-exposure vaccination for at-risk groups, and mass dog vaccination — the only intervention that eliminates human rabies at source.
evidence: Unambiguous: viral antigen and RNA in brain tissue of cases, with a complete chain of causation and a highly effective prophylactic intervention.
